name: Pediatric antegrade tibial elastic-nail entry approach
corridor: Paired medial and lateral proximal-metaphyseal cortical entries placed distal to physis and clear of tibial-tubercle apophysis

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with proximal tibia and entire leg accessible for orthogonal imaging and fracture manipulation.

setup.text: Mark proximal physis and tibial-tubercle apophysis fluoroscopically, select balanced nail diameters, and plan symmetric opposing bends and entries.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark proximal tibial physis, tibial tubercle/apophysis, medial and lateral metaphyseal cortices, fibular head, and anterior-compartment border.

incision.text: Create medial and lateral incisions beginning at planned entries and extending about 2 cm proximally to permit oblique nail insertion.

superficial_interval.text: Dissect directly to medial cortex; laterally retract proximal anterior-compartment muscle laterally and place entry slightly more anterior as needed.

deep_interval.text: Open paired metaphyseal cortices approximately 2 cm distal to proximal physis, avoiding tubercle cartilage, and angle each entry for controlled nail advancement.

layers.text: Skin, medial subcutaneous or lateral muscle-retraction plane, metaphyseal cortex, then medullary canal.

structures_encountered.text: Medial subcutaneous tibia, lateral anterior-compartment muscle, proximal metaphyseal cortex, physis, apophysis, and medullary canal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Proximal tibial physis, tibial-tubercle apophysis, common peroneal nerve near fibular neck, anterior-compartment muscle, skin at nail ends, and distal physis are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Keep both entries distal to proximal physis and clear of tibial-tubercle apophysis; avoid a far-lateral trajectory toward fibular head/common peroneal nerve.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract lateral muscle gently rather than dissecting posteriorly, and protect skin from prominent nail ends.

exposure.text: Provides paired metaphyseal portals for balanced antegrade elastic nails without crossing proximal physis.

limitations.text: Elastic nails provide limited control in highly comminuted, length-unstable, very proximal/distal, or near-mature patterns and commonly irritate entry sites.

extensions.text: Enlarge either incision only enough for safe cortical access or nail retrieval; add a limited fracture window if closed reduction fails.

indications.text: Use for selected unstable pediatric tibial diaphyseal fractures when acceptable alignment cannot be maintained nonoperatively.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose plate, rigid nail in appropriate maturity, or external fixation when fracture location/stability, soft tissue, or patient size makes ESIN control inadequate.

implant_implications.text: Use two balanced elastic nails with symmetric bends and opposing cortical support; leave ends accessible but not prominent beneath skin.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Verify both entry points below physis, nail progression, fracture length/rotation/alignment, and distal endpoints clear of physis in AP and lateral planes.

closure.text: Confirm nail ends are buried without skin pressure, obtain hemostasis, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin separately.

complications.text: Complications include entry-site irritation, skin breakdown, infection, malalignment, compartment syndrome, delayed union, nail migration, and physeal/apophyseal injury.

bailouts.text: Add a limited reduction incision or change fixation when balanced nails cannot restore and maintain acceptable length, rotation, and alignment.

procedure_applications.condition: An unstable pediatric tibial fracture requires operative fixation with paired antegrade elastic nails

questions.question: How far below the proximal physis are entries placed?
Why is the lateral entry more anterior?
questions.answer: To account for proximal anterior-compartment muscle coverage.

questions.question: Which cartilage must be avoided?
questions.answer: The proximal tibial physis and tibial-tubercle apophysis.
